Mission Control · Feature Guide

Mission Control: a local control plane for a fleet of coding agents

One dashboard that discovers, dispatches, watches, reviews, and ships the work of many Claude Code / Codex / Pi sessions at once - with an autonomous operator, a versioned review system, and a memory that outlives the checkout.

work in progress screenshots from a token-free demo fleet self-contained · opens from file://

In one paragraph

Mission Control is a local control plane for a fleet of coding agents. A single Node daemon on 127.0.0.1:7317 discovers every terminal-backed claude / codex / pi session on the machine, launches new ones into isolated git worktrees, and streams the whole fleet into one browser (or Electron) dashboard over Server-Sent Events. Around that core sit six systems that turn "many agents running" into "work that actually ships": Dispatch with typed task kinds, a Backlog fed by GitHub and Jira, Foreman (an autonomous operator that drains the needs-you queue), Workflows and Personas (versioned, auditable review runs with deterministic command gates and a GitHub Inspector), Retro and repository memory (what a session learned, committed into the repo it learned it about), and Ensembles (many agents on one task, judged blind).

Everything below is drawn from the repository at commit 4438b563. Every screenshot was captured from a real built daemon driving a token-free demo fleet, so the frames are of the product, not a mockup.

01The control plane and the Board

Mission Control has one job at the top level: answer what is this fleet doing, and what needs me? in a single look. The Board layout is the shape that answers it fastest - a column per state, with the backlog in front of them.

The top bar

The bar is fitted to exactly one row by measured rungs (src/web/topbarLadder.ts), so it degrades by collapsing labels to glyphs rather than wrapping. Reading left to right:

  • Page segments - ▦ Fleet (f), ⌗ Library (w), ▷ Runs (r), ⌖ Scouts (⇧S). Routes are hashes: #/fleet, #/library, #/runs, #/ensembles, #/scouts, #/shipped, #/settings/<category>. An unrecognized hash lands on #/fleet.
  • Filter (/) - a case-insensitive substring match over session name, displayed status label, and agent; and separately over a backlog task's title, status, agent and labels, so typing ghostty finds a queued task even when no session matches.
  • Fleet pulse - the connection word (live, reconnecting, or live · awake while Keep awake holds), session counts, need you, and a clickable to answer count that opens the attention inbox.
  • Spend chip - ≈$10.81 with an hourly rate, escalating amber then red as projected quota exhaustion approaches; its popover breaks down the Claude + Codex API-equivalent estimate, tokens, cost per pull request, and rate-limit runway, and attributes Foreman's and the Inspector's own model spend separately as automation.
  • Missions, the Foreman control, the primary Dispatch button (the one control that keeps its word at every width), the ⚙ gear carrying the worst settings-rail dot, and the alert bell (🔔 / 🔕 / 🌙).

The Line

Above every layout sits the Line: six stages in pipeline order - intake, backlog, working, review, decide, shipped (LINE_STAGES in src/shared/line.ts, append-only). Counts, tone and a one-sentence status are folded on the daemon and pushed as one change-gated line_summary event, so the browser never computes them and never polls. A stage goes amber only when a person must act; Shipped never does. Clicking a stage opens a drawer between the strip and the board - capped at three rows or 38vh, dismissed with a second click or Esc - except Working, which just clears the filter.

Layouts

Board is a column per tone; Console is a dense rail with one always-open detail. (A third, Cards/grid, is retired but existing preferences still render.) Columns come from TONE_GROUPS: needs you, working, idle, unconfirmed, gone. Empty columns are not treated alike - an empty needs you column keeps its place and renders an explicit All clear · Nothing is waiting on you, because that is worth saying out loud; every other empty column is stashed into the right-hand rail one click from coming back.

Opening a tile does not slide a drawer over the board. The clicked column morphs into a console rail of exactly that column's sessions and the detail grows into the freed space - reversible with Esc or the ‹ back button. One mental model, two densities.

What is on a card

identity

Agent, name, held

Brand dot, renameable name, and a held tag when a live workflow run owns the next turn.

why

Goal

One sentence - what this session is currently trying to solve - derived from your own prompts by a local model call and refreshed as you steer it.

now

Activity ticker

⟳ running Bash, from observed tool invocations.

progress

Stage ladder

A cropped rung of the bound workflow's ladder with a disclosure (e expands it in place).

marks

Flags row

◈ Agent SDK, Foreman ◆ decision / ✎ draft, review, N queued, a real PR link, the Inspector chip, recurring-mission origin, ensemble mark.

economics

Runtime line

Model, thinking level, a context meter with its percentage, the effort and permission-mode pickers, and a cost chip.

Session state words come from one function (stateDisplay): exited, stopping, N to review, needs an answer (a pane dialog, read straight off the terminal, which is why it outranks the hooks-confidence split), the transient interrupting, running when unconfirmed, then starting | working | idle | needs input | needs review.

Backlog cards drag onto genuinely free tiles. A refused drop is reported on the board; a handover that would reset an agent still holding a queue or a branch raises a confirmation reconciled against the live lists rather than against what the page believed when the drag started.

Attention, alerts, and away mode

Alerts fire only on transitions into blocked-on-you states, with a synthesized Web Audio chime, so a fleet that has been waiting for an hour does not keep shouting. Four deterministic stuck-session rules break through even while away. Away mode is daemon state, not a browser preference: it buffers everything else and hands you one digest when you come back. Sitrep (⇧P) is the whole-fleet snapshot as a panel, and the same content is available as JSON at GET /api/report and markdown at /api/report.md.

02The session desk: conversation, diff, files

Click a tile and you are at the desk for one agent. One component (ConsoleDetail) serves both layouts, keyed by session id, so switching sessions remounts cleanly. Its header carries the agent dot, a renameable title, the goal line, then the PR / Inspector / workflow / ensemble / pipeline chips, the ＋ workflow bind chip, the state badge, and a runtime cluster led by the permission-mode picker - posture first, because model, context and cost are all consequences of it.

Five tabs, in the order the strip draws them and the keyboard walks them, each printing the chord that also reveals it:

TabChordWhat it answers
ConversationgWhat has this agent said and done, and what do I need to answer?
Work queueqWhat is it about to do next? (pip = open items)
WorkflowsyHow is the review run going?
DiffdWhat did it actually change?
Files⇧FLet me read or edit the tree myself.

At the far end of the strip sits the Foreman rail - ＋ Invite foreman, Foreman intent, or Foreman · N with an attention dot. Deliberately not a tab: it is a consent boundary, not a view of the work.

Conversation

Anything you must answer is hoisted above the transcript - a pane-dialog prompt for a menu the session is parked on, a Foreman escalation strip - because a question buried in scrollback is a question you will miss. The transcript renders two ways: as a terminal stream (the default) or as a chat log with grey tool chips. Four voices are colour-coded: the agent's accent, your blue, Foreman's purple, and gold review answers placed at the moment you answered them. A second rail mode, Yours, indexes your own messages and dims non-operator user turns - useful because roughly half of "user" turns in an agent transcript are harness scaffolding, not a person.

The composer writes into Mission Control's own editable outbox on both runtimes. Messages appear as You · queued turns; ↑ in an empty box recalls the newest editable one; an unprovable terminal delivery becomes delivery uncertain and offers Retry or Mark sent rather than pretending. Placeholders state why you cannot type - "No pane to send to", "Waiting on a menu - pick an option above to answer it".

Permission modes go through one picker that drives each harness's native control: Claude's manual / accept edits / plan plus bypass / auto / don't ask, Codex's Ask for approval / Approve for me / Full Access / Read Only. It renders read-only when the pane cannot be written. Questions arrive as clickable rows; a multi-select AskUserQuestion becomes a checkbox form with Submit answers; the MCP tools request_input, request_plan_decisions and request_review block the agent until you answer. Interrupt (⌃C) stops the turn and drops the queue only when a turn was genuinely stopped.

Diff

The patch is computed on the daemon, not in the browser, and how it picks its base is the whole point:

  1. Resolve the repository toplevel, because patch paths are toplevel-relative and that matters in a monorepo.
  2. Pick a source ref: refs/remotes/origin/HEAD, else origin/main|master, else local main|master.
  3. Diff from merge-base(HEAD, ref) - so the mainline's newer commits stay out of your agent's diff.

No shared history falls back to working-tree-vs-HEAD. An explicitly requested base must equal that merge-base or the call fails closed with "base commit … is not reachable" - a wrong diff is worse than no diff. An unborn HEAD skips the tracked half; untracked files render as new files through read-only --no-index; oversized patches are clipped and flagged truncated rather than silently shortened. The reader heads itself honestly: branch vs base, working tree vs base, uncommitted changes, or fix <sha>. File rows are walked with arrows or j/k, and a row that cannot open in Files (a deleted file, one outside the working directory) is aria-disabled with the reason.

Files

Editing is real, and conflict handling is explicit: if the file changed underneath you the panel offers Compare / Reload / overwrite / Copy local instead of picking for you. Markdown Preview renders bounded mermaid fences locally, in a no-network sandbox.

Workflows and the work queue

Terminal is not a tab. The launchers in the tab strip open a login shell in the worktree across tmux / cmux / WezTerm / Ghostty - and unavailable backends are listed with the reason rather than hidden. The agent button focuses a live pane, opens Continue in terminal (⇧T) for an embedded session, or resumes an exited one.

Per-session actions live in the footer bar: terminal / handoff, focus, diff, reset, retro, interrupt, complete, kill - plus rename and invite/withdraw Foreman. The Foreman invite never writes optimistically, and a refusal says what is still true rather than what failed.

03Dispatch and task kinds

+ or the top bar's Dispatch button opens one dialog that does two jobs: launch an agent now, or shelve the work in the backlog. By default it opens on the guided pass - a keyboard walk through four questions inside the same dialog, which then hands you the ordinary form with those answers set and the caret in the task box.

StepChoicesKeys
RepoEvery repository in the workspace, seeded from your last dispatchtype to filter, ↑↓, ↵
Kindship, scout, plan, pipeline (conductor-enabled repos only), chatp t l e c, arrows, or a position digit
HarnessClaude Code, Codex, Pic x i
After workDispatch default, None, or any active published Workflowd n, the printed Workflow letter

The full form is eight controls: Repo (plus + Add another repo), the task composer, a Crew row of Agent / Kind / Model / Effort, After work, and a Backlog details fold holding priority, labels, title, the autopilot switch and dependencies - whose summary row names what is set (no priority · no labels · title summarized · autopilot on · no dependencies) so the fold never hides a decision.

Runtime is not a per-task field. Each harness card in Settings carries a Session runtime select - Terminal or Agent SDK - and the daemon resolves it once per launch. A task cannot ask for a runtime its harness does not offer.

Leave Title blank and the daemon derives one with a tool-less Haiku call before dispatch, because the title supplies both the git branch name and the session name. Choosing scout, plan or chat moves After work to None - none of them produces a reviewable diff - and hands the earlier choice back if you switch to ship.

Multi-repo attach

+ Add another repo attaches secondary repositories, and one dispatch still produces one session. Its cwd is the primary repo's worktree; each attached repo gets its own worktree on the same branch name. Write access is granted at launch (Claude --add-dir, Codex writable sandbox roots) and the request is refused for a harness without multiRepoDispatch rather than silently degraded. The intent is prefixed with a manifest naming each worktree, which one is primary, and each branch. Provisioning is all-or-nothing. Consequences: Foreman needs every repo allowlisted, multi-repo tasks are dispatch-only (never draggable onto a running agent), each repo's PR is tracked separately, and completion requires every changed repo to have merged - one pull request per repository.

What happens on dispatch

POST /api/tasks validates the body, resolves the repo set, refuses multi-repo for an incapable harness, checks the workflow selection, refuses a plan dispatch whose skills cannot be invoked, and creates the task. The dispatcher then, in order: clears stale error state, derives branch and home names, resolves the pinned base commit, resolves the runtime once, enforces multiRepoDispatch, provisions all worktrees (a native pool slot, or a disposable git worktree on a fresh harness/… branch) recording them before spawning anything, appends the task-kind contract and any repository-memory pointer, and takes exactly one launch path:

  • Terminal - launches claude/codex/pi in a terminal home rooted at the worktree, waits for the discovered session, then injects the task. Timings are tunable: DISPATCH_READY_MS (30s), DISPATCH_HOOK_READY_MS (20s), DISPATCH_SETTLE_MS (2s), DISPATCH_ACCEPT_MS (15s).
  • Agent SDK - starts the embedded driver with the task as turn one. No terminal home, no discovery, no paste; the driver's binding is the readiness signal.
If either path cannot prove it started as requested, the dispatch fails rather than reporting a task as running. This is the single most load-bearing rule in dispatch: a fleet dashboard that lies about what is running is worse than no dashboard.

The five task kinds

The registry is TASK_KINDS, append-only, and array order is picker order. ship is index 0 and the default. Copy lives in TASK_KIND_INFO; behaviour in TASK_KIND_BEHAVIOR. This is the whole set:

idWhat it is forDeliverableDiff?Backlog?Extra MCP tools
shipDeliver a changeA merged pull requestyesyesnone
scoutInvestigate and reportA self-contained static report page, archivednoyessubmit_scout_artifacts
planProduce a reviewed planA plan PR, plus scheduled phase tasksnoyesrequest_plan_decisions, create_task
pipelineRun conductor's external SDLC pipelineWhatever the engine shipsnoyesnone
chatOpen-ended conversationNone - the conversation is the pointnononone

ship

The silent default: no kind badge is drawn on the card, because most work is this. It is the only kind that produces a reviewable diff, so it is the only kind an after-work review Workflow is preselected for.

scout

A scout's prompt is appended by the daemon, not by a skill, and it is a contract: write one self-contained static page at docs/reports/<slug>/report.html - inline CSS, inline SVG, data: URIs, no JavaScript, no external request of any kind, must open from file:// - then hand it over with submit_scout_artifacts. A scout cannot be marked done, and its worktree is not reclaimed, until Mission Control has captured and verified that page into an archive. No PR is expected; Foreman's automatic wrap-up retires a scout's completion without submitting a workflow or raising a "Ship it?" card. This guide is itself a scout report.

plan

A plan's appended contract: write docs/plans/<name>/plan.md with a rendered plan.html, invoke the html-plans skill, ask for review and every open choice through request_plan_decisions, and end by invoking the phased-plan skill to schedule one dependency-linked backlog task per phase via create_task. Both skills must be enabled or the dispatch is refused on the form (backlogging is still allowed; the check is re-asked at launch). Unlike a scout, a plan lands as a PR, and its plan directories are captured to the archive library before any checkout is destroyed.

pipeline

The only kind whose launch owner is not a harness. Conductor owns the worktree, agent, model, effort, and every downstream agent, so Agent / Model / Effort / attached repos / After work are all unavailable, and the provider owns task completion. It is the only kind restricted to conductor-enabled repositories, and it is excluded from backlog autopilot.

chat

The only kind refused from the backlog - "Chat tasks must be launched immediately from Dispatch." It cannot carry dependencies, be created by a recurring mission or a task source, or be an ensemble member. Only Dispatch now is offered.

04The backlog and task sources

The backlog is the fleet's staging area: everything that should happen but has not been launched. It is deliberately a plain list of rows with a status, not a second scheduler.

Lifecycle

Task status is backlog | dispatching | running | done | cancelled | failed - deliberately not the session's runtime state, which is a different question with a different answer.

  • Priorities are low, med, high, blocker, ranked 0, 2, 3, 4 with unset = 1, so an unset priority sorts above Low. Pure annotation, editable at any status.
  • Labels are free strings, trimmed, case-insensitively deduped (first spelling wins), capped at 32 characters and 12 per task.
  • Dependencies are task refs (durable) or bare session refs, each with a snapshot of the prerequisite's title and a persisted satisfiedAt. An unmet dependency forces the task into the backlog and releases only when the prerequisite's PR is observed merged - every changed repo, for a multi-repo task. Cycles are refused. A stopped prerequisite surfaces a warning offering Reschedule or Mark done.
  • Hold is a per-task enabled column. Foreman's ready list never sees a parked item, and the daemon refuses /dispatch and /assign unless the request claims overrideDisabled - which the dashboard does and Foreman never does. Parked items still count against the planning budget, so parking is not hiding.

Backlog autopilot

Autopilot lives in the Foreman control, not on the backlog, because it is Foreman doing the work. It reads the planning head - the first 400 items, held ones included - and schedules enabled ready items one at a time: preferring a genuinely free agent (settled, hook-instrumented, has a pane, no queue, no pending review, no open PR, same repo, same harness - reset first) over cutting a fresh worktree, never past Max agents running at once (default 3), and only in Live mode on an allowlisted repository.

Inferred dependencies come from one tool-less model call and are then sanitized: unknown ids dropped, self-references dropped, only cycle-closing edges cut, forgotten items appended unblocked. Operator-declared edges are authoritative and cannot be reversed by the model. Three consecutive planner failures degrade to serial oldest-first scheduling with a 10-minute retry probe.

Vocabulary that matters. A work queue feeds an existing session. The backlog provisions a new one. They are different tables and different machines.

Where work comes from

Eight distinct sources file backlog rows, and the guarantee they share is that none of them launches an agent:

1 · the form

Dispatch

Add to backlog, or the edit path when you click a shelved task and reopen the same form.

2 · agents

MCP create_task

Always ship, claude, backlog: true, with dependsOnTaskIds and dependsOnCurrentSession. This is the tool the phased-plan skill uses to file one task per phase.

3 · your tracker

Task sources

GitHub issues and Jira JQL filters, swept on a schedule.

4 · the clock

Recurring missions

A cron schedule that files a backlog task and stops.

5 · hindsight

Retro follow-ups

Retro: <session name>, filed when the session that learned something can no longer take a turn.

6 · ensembles

Member and replacement tasks

Created internally; they opt out of the machine-wide After work default.

7 · the tour

Product-tour routes

A fixed demo ship task and a fixed chat task, through the ordinary manual-dispatch capability.

8 · outward

Push to GitHub

The one direction that leaves: a shelved task becomes an issue, and the seen-ledger row plus the task's link are written in one transaction so the next sweep cannot re-file it.

Task sources in detail

Two kinds ship: github-issues and jira. Per source you configure Enable, which repository tasks are filed against, sweep interval (1 min - 24 h, default 15), max tasks per sweep (default 25), and the swept-task template (agent, kind, priority, labels, whether autopilot may touch them) - plus Sweep now, Check it works (a preflight), and Forget seen items.

  • GitHub authenticates through the gh CLI in the repository. Filters: repository, labels (any of), assignee, milestone, issues per sweep, copy labels, priority from a label.
  • Jira points at a JQL filter. Auth is a ladder - the jira CLI, else JIRA_API_TOKEN + JIRA_EMAIL. REST pages to 1000 issues / 50 requests, and the token is only ever sent to *.atlassian.net unless JIRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS names the host.

Ingestion is the single writer, and it is deliberately dull: drop anything already seen by (source_id, external_id) against a task_source_seen table - not against live tasks, so deleting a task keeps it deleted - resolve and validate the repo root, normalize through the same dispatch schema the form uses, cap at maxPerSweep reporting the overflow, create the task, and record the seen row in the same transaction. A sweep never re-syncs an item that changed upstream: the backlog is yours once the row exists.

Recurring missions

A mission's schedule keeps a cron expression (five fields), a timezone, overlap and missed-run policies, a revision, and a durable next_run_at cursor. An occurrences table is the exactly-once ledger, keyed UNIQUE (schedule_id, scheduled_for) with the task id preallocated at claim time. A due instant files a backlog task and stops. Missed-run policy is coalesce-to-latest (default), create-all (capped at 50 per catch-up), or skip; overlap policy is skip-if-active (default) or allow. Minimum interval is one hour.

05Foreman, the autonomous operator

The dashboard can tell you who needs you. Foreman is the answer to and who will deal with it. It is a single background agent that drains the work a human would otherwise drain by hand, and it has two halves.

  • Reactive - it reads each blocked session's transcript and its terminal screen, auto-answers the routine calls, escalates genuine forks as a framed decision brief, and writes a one-or-two-sentence Purpose onto every session card it inspects.
  • Proactive - per-session work queues, fleet-wide backlog autopilot, pull-request follow-through, and completion wrap-up.
Why it reads the screen and not just the transcript. A prompt that is waiting on a human - a menu, a permission dialog - is not written to the transcript until it returns, so the transcript routinely ends before the question. The screen is also how a menu is answered: a dialog discards typed characters and the following Enter confirms whichever row was highlighted. So Foreman walks the cursor onto its chosen row and presses Enter only while the pane still shows that row selected - and an answer it cannot pin to a visible row is escalated rather than typed.

Consent is separate from capability

Two different questions, two different answers. Can Foreman drive this session - do the harness's hooks let it observe and act? And may it - does the session carry an invite? Invites are sdk (embedded), dispatch (dispatched terminals), operator (explicitly invited), or null. In an uninvited session Foreman does nothing - no Purpose, no brief, no queue tick, no wrap-up, no backlog assignment - and the daemon refuses Foreman-marked writes into uninvited panes a second time at its own boundary. An operator invite grants everything except backlog assignment: helping with what a session is already doing is not permission to start something else in it.

The control you actually use

Foreman ships enabled but inert: enabled defaults true (it is a gate a workflow's Foreman-complete binding requires), mode defaults dry-run, the repository allowlist defaults empty, and the worker is a separate process nothing starts for you - npm run foreman.

The worker

The worker never opens SQLite. Everything it does goes over the daemon's loopback API - config, sessions, reviews, pane, transcript, diff, standards, send, inject, select-option, submit-options, note, episode, queue, task dispatch/assign, backlog plan. The daemon remains the only database writer, and even the worker's spend spool is a plain buffer file that owns no schema.

main() is one loop: sweep the durable spend outbox (30s), read config, resolve the provider and transport, publish planner health, bail if disabled or if this process is not the lease leader, snapshot sessions and reviews, run the fleet-level steps (backlog autopilot, pipeline triage, review follow-up) even when there are no targets, then walk each target with 400 ms between sessions - re-reading config between them so a mid-drain disable takes effect immediately.

Only one worker ever drives sessions. A compare-and-swap lease in app_config (90 s TTL) is renewed by a background timer every 30 s, deliberately decoupled from loop progress because a single tick can block on a model call for minutes. A second npm run foreman acquires nothing and idles as a standby, taking over automatically.

How a decision gets made

Every session is judged in a fresh, tool-less headless call. A cheap tier sits in front of the expensive reviewer:

TierWhat it isWhat it may do
0Pure code, freeA plan or diff review is structurally human-only, so it is disposed with a Purpose and no model call at all.
1A Haiku router over a trimmed 12-turn windowBuckets the ask rather than solving it. Asymmetric: it may skip or escalate freely, but may auto-answer only routine-access.
2The full reviewer (Opus by default)Returns purpose, classification, action, answer, recommendation, brief, confidence - converted into a note plus at most one send.

Five code backstops sit behind the router and it cannot override any of them: a destructive-pattern denylist (rm -rf, force-push, --no-verify, reset --hard, drop table, sudo, secrets/.env, prod deploy, skip ci…), confidence below 0.6, an unscannable window counted as unknown rather than safe, an unresolvable window boundary, and menu delivery - the router's schema has no option field, so its answer to a menu routes up to the reviewer that can name a row.

Because a review can take minutes, any plan that "leaves a mark" is re-checked against a fresh snapshot; a verdict whose ask has already closed is filed as stale rather than pinned onto a session that has moved on.

Durable posture and the ledger

Standing instructions are the prose half - seeded from a shipped brief, stored in app config, edited at #/library/personas/foreman, saved compare-and-swap against an ETag. Three durable states: built-in default, customized, and an intentional empty none that does not fall back. They reach review, verify and the cheap tier, framed as direction rather than evidence, under a one-way ratchet: they may raise Foreman's bar, never lower it, never authorize a destructive act, widen approval authority, retire an escalation rule, or dictate literal text sent to a session.

Every decision is kept as an episode - the verbatim ask, the captured screen, the brief, the recommendation, the resolution, the tier and the reason it took that tier, credited to whoever made the call. Outcomes are answered, drafted, escalated, declined, stale, dismissed; the ledger holds 100 rows with 30-day retention. Token spend is accounted separately: one function prices and writes every automation run, so Foreman and the Inspector cannot drift. Reports are buffered durably before the first attempt, keyed on run id so retries cannot double-count, erased only on a definitive answer, and quarantined rather than dropped when the daemon cannot price them.

What it will never do

  • Open SQLite.
  • Type into a session it was not invited into.
  • Send outside Live mode on an allowlisted repository (a blank allowlist entry cannot grant everything).
  • Auto-approve a destructive or risky ask, whatever the router or the standing instructions say.
  • Type an answer at a menu it cannot pin to a visible row.
  • Run tests as verification. Queue-item verification is evidence-only, reading that item's own diff and transcript against the repository's own AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md; only blocking gaps send the agent back, under a per-gap budget of 3 attempts and a hard stop of 10 rounds.
  • Create a pull request from the CI or review-nudge path.
  • Act at the same time as a second worker.

Overrides are all direct: answer the ask yourself and the note retires with it; press Dismiss; flip the mode back to dry-run; withdraw the invite; or stop the worker - at which point Foreman is enabled and idle, and the panel says exactly that, in words.

06Workflows, Personas, and shipping

A workflow turns a repeatable review process into durable, auditable runs. It is authored once, published as an immutable version, bound to a session, and then it judges that session's work, sends repair instructions back, and drives the pull request itself.

The Library

Authoring surfaces mount one level deeper - #/library/workflows, /personas, /actions, /commands, each with a /<id> deep link and a /new blank draft. Execution lives on separate top-level pages: #/runs, #/ensembles, #/shipped. Every legacy #/workflows/* spelling still parses and rewrites the address bar, permanently.

The ladder

The Pipeline view models a workflow as a linear ladder, Session → stage 1 → … → End. Two stage kinds exist and the difference is what they do to the run:

  • An evaluation stage holds one or more Persona reviewers and/or deterministic Command nodes. All members read the same submission; a stage of two or more gets an all-pass Join and advances only when every member passes. Its seam is pass / fail.
  • A session action stage holds exactly one action and no members. It does not judge - it sends an authored instruction into the bound session, waits for that turn, and captures fresh evidence for everything below it. Its only seam is complete.

The Graph view edits anything, under validation that encodes real costs: a Join needs both outcomes from at least two distinct predecessors and may never be fed by an action (an action produces no verdict to aggregate), and cycles are legal only when they pass through Session - a Persona-only cycle could spend model calls repeatedly against unchanged work.

Drafts autosave after 500 ms of quiet, and every write carries the revision it loaded, so a stale tab is offered Reload latest or Duplicate my draft rather than overwriting. Publish creates an immutable version freezing every Persona's exact name, description, Markdown, provider/model overrides and revision - and for actions, the instruction, the required skill, the completion, and the source revision. Editing a Persona afterwards cannot reach a published version; history simply marks the snapshot outdated. Archive is soft and refused while a binding is active; Delete is offered only for a workflow that was never published, because no version means no binding, no run, nothing to orphan.

How a run progresses

Bind a session to an exact published version, then submit - Preview (no keystrokes, no delivery, no Foreman or Inspector action) or Live. Every submit carries a durable request key and the daemon creates the submission row before evidence capture, so a retry returns the same row.

One submission captures one shared snapshot for every concurrent Persona: raw goal, refined goal, human decisions and rationale, repository HEAD and diff, transcript evidence, repository standards, and prior Persona feedback. Persona prompts put operator intent, decisions, constraints and acceptance criteria before repository evidence; all captured evidence is fenced as untrusted; prior Persona feedback is labelled non-human. Transcript budgeting is per-turn (8,000 UTF-8 bytes, head+tail with exact omitted-byte counts), filled newest-to-oldest.

Malformed output, provider failures and timeouts are infrastructure errors, never fail verdicts. A reviewer that could not report is not a reviewer that said no. The whole daemon runs at most three review calls at once, shared between Persona attempts and context compaction.

Failures return to Session as one bounded, deterministic repair packet in published graph order, carrying only the failed findings. Repair resumption is an immutable per-version policy: under auto the daemon reopens the next round itself once the session has settled and the repository changed or new evidence was staged - deliberately not on a transcript that merely grew. Max repair rounds is the budget; exhausting it blocks the run, and only Grant 2 more rounds on the run page can reach a live run's budget. A reviewer that rejects the same work two rounds running raises an edge-triggered repeat offender alert.

Gates

Command nodes name a portable slot - test, lint, typecheck, build - never an argv, so a workflow travels between repositories. Each slot gets one machine-wide default plus per-repository exceptions. It runs as argv (no shell) in a pooled worktree pinned to the captured commit, under a supervisor that can prove the process group is gone. Non-zero exit fails the submission and returns the command's own output as the repair packet. An unconfigured, unauthorized or unsupported-platform slot reports Not run and passes with a note - which is exactly what the screenshots above show. Infrastructure faults retry and then block; they never fail. Consent is gated twice: a machine-wide "Allow workflow Commands" switch and the repository's Workflows cell in Settings → Trust.

Personas

Five review roles ship, ids builtin:<slug>:

PersonaIts one job
Intent Conformance JudgeDoes the change contradict a stated acceptance criterion? Fails only on a removed required behavior or an added forbidden one.
Code Risk ReviewerRisk the changed code introduces - bugs, security, performance, breaking changes, error handling. Never style, formatting, linting or types.
Test Evidence AuditorDoes the evidence show the intent working end to end? Visual evidence is required for anything a user sees.
Documentation StewardWhat documentation did this change make stale, under a one-owner-per-fact placement policy.
Code Quality JudgeThe final local judgment - correctness, security, resource lifetime, error handling, compatibility, regression evidence - before a PR exists.

Each attempt is a fresh, tool-less provider call, and the actual runner and model are recorded on the attempt. Resolution order: the Persona's provider override or the app-wide provider, then the Persona's model override, then an env override, then that provider's balanced default. Built-ins are read-only with reserved names; Duplicate to edit yields an ordinary Persona that upgrades never touch. Operators can also Import .md or Import from path, in which case the daemon records provenance - source path, enclosing worktree, plugin version, sha256, import time - and Check upstream raises upstream changed / source missing badges. Stored guidance never changes automatically; adopting drift is an explicit new revision.

Session actions and their contracts

CompletionWhat must be observed
session_turnThe session verifiably picked the instruction up, then settled. A pre-existing idle never counts.
pull_requestThat turn boundary, plus an adopted, open PR on this repository root and branch whose last-polled remote head equals the exact commit the continuation captured - full object ids, abbreviations resolved against the object database.
repo_commitThat turn boundary, plus a commit in the bound checkout made after pickup.

While a PR action waits it names one of four states - Awaiting PR, Awaiting push, PR on another repo, PR on another branch - all of which are waits. Only a PR at the reviewed commit that is closed or merged actually blocks, and a blocked action writes no verdict, sends no repair packet, and spends no repair round. Two actions ship: builtin:pull-request and builtin:retro.

The built-in workflow

No-Mistakes Review, currently version 10 (versions 1-9 preserved for pinned bindings), compiled into the build rather than seeded into your database:

  1. Commands typecheck + test behind an all-pass Join - a change that does not compile costs zero model calls.
  2. intent-conformance-judge alone - the cheap drift gate.
  3. code-risk-reviewer + code-quality-judge in parallel behind a Join.
  4. test-evidence-auditor + documentation-steward in parallel behind a Join.
  5. The builtin:pull-request session action, whose complete route reaches End only once an open PR is verified at the captured commit.

Evidence submission

A workflow-bound ship task whose graph contains a Persona may register bounded image and text evidence before completion, through submit_workflow_evidence. Each entry names a stable client id, a checkout-relative path, a required caption, and a repository scope that is either an issued slot (repo-01) or all - and all is authorized only when the task received that scope. The daemon resolves the slot from the task itself; the agent never names a session, task, or root. It rejects paths outside the checkout, symlinks, non-files, unsupported images, and files that are not gitignored. Capture happens inside the conversation capture lock: sources are opened without following symlinks, re-hashed, re-sniffed, and copied into submission-owned immutable storage before any Persona spend. Personas receive images as ordered native inputs plus an untrusted manifest carrying ids, captions, scopes, MIME types, sizes and digests - and no local paths.

The GitHub Inspector

The Inspector is the optional remote reviewer, separate from the local Code Quality Judge. It reviews only the pull requests Mission Control opened, against the reviewed repository's own personas/INSPECTOR.md (falling back to a root INSPECTOR.md), leaves inline comments, answers replies in its own threads, re-reviews every push, resolves its own threads when a push fixes them, and posts one top-level "safe to merge" comment when a live review finds nothing and every earlier finding is resolved. It never approves and never requests changes.

Adoption is the consent model: a PR is adopted when the hook saw the agent run gh pr create - matched on the command, not the output, because gh pr view prints the same URL - or when a projected external pipeline writes a pr_url whose owner and repository match a GitHub remote in that checkout. Sniffed URLs adopt nothing. Adoption is not consent to post; that is mode plus the Trust allowlist. Own-comment identity requires both the authenticated login and a hidden marker at the very start of the body (quote replies prefix > , so start position matters).

The reading grant is declared per harness rather than assumed: on Claude, one fresh query with Read/Grep/Glob in the reviewed worktree, bounded by a read-only allowlist, path deny rules (.env*, keys, .ssh, .aws, .git/config, Mission Control state), a rule that every finding must name a file the PR changed, and a secret scrubber on every outbound string. On Codex there is no grant at all - the runner declares it can sandbox none, so the review reads only the diff in the prompt. A workflow can also require a published Inspector final gate: after a successful End the run waits until a normal Inspector sweep, observed after gate entry, proves the open PR's remote head equals the captured committed HEAD with a clean tree.

07Retro, memory, and archives

Three features answering one question: what survives a session? A retro turns a finished session into durable knowledge, repository memory is where that knowledge is committed, and archives are where a session's reports and plans outlive the checkout that produced them.

Retro

A retro is not a report. Its product is at most three durable memories, committed into the repository they are about, plus optionally a deletion or a promotion. The governing rule, enforced by every arm of the routing code: nothing is written that a human did not approve, and the commit is the agent's - Mission Control never writes to a repository, and the daemon never commits.

Retro is a session action, not a task kind - the built-in builtin:retro, whose contract is requiredSkill: retro plus completion: repo_commit. That completion is deliberate: a retrospective that discussed three memories and wrote none has not completed. Because the skill is the human-approval ceremony, every retro path fails closed while that skill is switched off, including paths that type nothing.

One route, no body: POST /api/sessions/:id/retro. It resolves by durable pull-request posture first, then reachability:

OutcomeMeaning
deliveredTyped into the live session that did the work - it already holds the context.
dispatchedThe session cannot take a turn, so a backlog retro task is filed naming session, branch and PR.
startedThe work PR already merged, so one linked follow-up task is created (or reused) and dispatched with fresh worktrees. The source task stays done.
queuedA linked follow-up exists but the launch was refused retryably; the reason is bounded to 400 characters.
409The retro skill is off, the source task is not yet done, no repository resolves, or a linked task needs cleanup.
503Live session, write failed; the body carries pasted, because false is safe to retry and true means the packet is sitting unsent in the composer.

Merged-PR posture beats reachability, and the post-merge follow-up is durable: a table enforces one retro task per (source_task_id, source_episode_id), so repeated clicks return the same task. Foreman does not trigger retros. Nothing in the daemon delivers one autonomously; the server only ever offers and a human always clicks.

What the retro agent does

  1. Reads the session back from the transcript, not from recollection - over loopback, bounded to 200 turns - looking for corrections the human had to type, avoidable cost, and review findings that were real. Two honesty constraints are stated up front: roughly half of "user" turns are harness scaffolding, and a retro on one's own work is a charitable reviewer.
  2. Chooses at most three. Three is a ceiling, not a target. It reads the existing memory index first, because restating an existing memory is not a proposal. Disqualified as defects: secrets, per-user paths or ports, anything the root doc already says, facts about the feature just built, anything not observed.
  3. Asks before writing, through request_plan_decisions.
  4. Writes only the approved files, updates the index line, validates index against directory, bootstraps the root-doc reference line once, and commits.

The approval form renders in the dashboard and blocks until the human submits or dismisses. The skill mandates that plan carry the full proposed text of every memory, exactly as it would be committed - showing a summary and committing something else is a breach - and one decision per proposed memory, never one listing all three, with options Commit this memory / Skip it and free text allowed. That free text is what makes this approve / edit / reject rather than yes-or-no: obedience is literal. add with no text commits exactly what was shown; add with text means their wording wins; skip writes nothing and is not raised again; dismissing writes nothing at all. If the MCP form is unavailable, the skill requires asking the same questions in conversation, in full - losing the form is not permission to skip the ceremony.

A post-merge retro that approves nothing must not manufacture a commit to look shipped. Its exit is complete_retro_no_change, a tool with an empty input schema - it accepts no task id and no arbitrary outcome. The daemon attributes the session itself, proves the task owns a retro relation, and completes only that task with a fixed outcome string. Repeating the call replays idempotently.

When the dashboard offers one

One predicate, in one file, so no two surfaces disagree - and nothing is ever drawn disabled; the offer appears only at its moment. Both halves must hold: the session is worth retrospecting (there was a human correction beyond the opening brief, or resolved Inspector findings) and review has finished (the bound run's gate reads clean, or the session's own Inspector chip does). The Complete dialog drops the second half - a scout or a spike never opens a PR - and offers "Run a retro first" instead. The corrections half is computed incrementally over the append-only transcript, sticky (a flipped session is never re-read), guarded by one stat, polled every 10 s by default.

Repository memory

The store lives in the repository the memory is about, never in Mission Control - because Mission Control's state is instance-local, and the whole point is that cloning the repo gets you the memory:

<repo>/
  AGENTS.md            # or CLAUDE.md - carries one reference line
  .agents/memory/
    MEMORY.md          # the index: one line per memory, with a link
    <slug>.md          # one memory per file, with front matter

Those two paths are a contract, not configuration: add, never rename. MEMORY.md is an index, not the corpus - a repository with fifty memories costs fifty lines of context, not fifty documents. Each entry carries front matter (category, date, source-session, times-confirmed) then a heading and one concrete paragraph of what happens and what to do instead.

Only the retro writes them, on the current branch, in the repository the memory is about, only its own files, with no co-author trailer. Riding the session's own branch means the memory is reviewed in the same PR as the work. The first retro in a repository bootstraps the root doc: resolve symlinks (a CLAUDE.md → AGENTS.md repo is one document with two names), search for the marker string, and if absent append exactly one line telling future agents to read the index. Present means done - that marker is the idempotence check.

ConsumerChannel
Claude, CodexLoad the root doc natively; the reference line instructs the read.
PiNo file channel, so dispatch prepends a memory pointer to turn one.
Inspector, workflow Personas, Foreman verifyThe index is part of the standards bundle.

The pointer is added only when the worktree actually carries an index, verified by realpath + stat with containment inside the repository - a MEMORY.md symlinked out of the tree is ignored everywhere, because repository content is untrusted input. Reviewers read the index and never open the topic files, and they run without file tools, which drives two rules: an index line that is only a link is a line they cannot follow, so say what the memory is; and memory is read last under the standards caps (24 KB per document, 64 KB per bundle), so at the cap memory is dropped first and the prompt says documents were omitted.

Curation is explicit. times-confirmed starts at 1; a retro confirming an existing memory increments it and changes nothing else, and a climbing count is the signal to promote into the root doc and delete the memory - one copy, never two. Deletion is a first-class outcome: a memory the session disproved, or whose trap was fixed, should go. Before committing, every .md beside the index must have exactly one index line and every line must point at a file that exists, because a drifted index is worse than none. Long procedural recipes are proposed as a repo-local skill instead, since a skill loads only on its trigger.

Archives

An archive is work kept as ordinary files, not rows. Two kinds are produced:

  • scout - an answer to a question. Handed over with submit_scout_artifacts, which needs both the harness token and a daemon-signed credential scoped to the current task checkout. Files beside the report are captured automatically; named supporting files land under artifacts/<repo-slot>/.
  • plan - docs/plans/<name>/plan.html becomes the report, with the rest of the directory beside it. There is no submission tool: the task's own git diff against its source branch decides which plan directories are archived, so a plan task cannot aim capture at a file it did not write. Plans are captured at teardown - reclaim, remove, cancel, reschedule, and the startup pass - not at completion.

Layout is archives/<producer-id>/<archive-id>/{manifest.json, report/, artifacts/}, and both directory levels are generated UUIDs - nothing an operator or an agent typed becomes a directory name. The manifest carries kind, producer, display and search metadata, timing, a capture status of complete or partial, byte sizes, SHA-256 digests, a content digest over a canonical file table, and a bounded human prompt trail. Task ids, session ids and absolute home paths are deliberately absent. The report must fetch nothing on open, and a non-executing parser refuses scripts, handlers, frames, <base>, meta refresh and any fetch-on-open URL slot.

Why the archive outlives the checkout. Because it is not a row. SQLite holds a disposable index that a background reconciler rebuilds - at startup after the port is already serving, on a filesystem hint, then on a jittered 60 s cadence - costing one stat for an unchanged bundle, and requiring two identical observations before verifying so a half-synced copy never flashes up as corrupt. Delete the database and restart: the whole catalog, including full report-text and prompt search, is rebuilt in the background and nothing is lost. Bundles are immutable and portable - drop one in from another machine and it appears within one cadence, validated as untrusted input.

Cleanup asks first: every path that destroys a checkout publishes the task's archives before deleting it, stopping a launched agent first so capture sees final bytes, and refuses the cleanup if capture fails for a retryable reason - the worktree stays and you retry. Deleting a task or reclaiming its worktree never deletes an archive, and there is no retention sweep. Deletion requires echoing the archive key in the request body, renames the bundle into .trash as its durable step, and touches no task, session, or repository.

08Ensembles

An ensemble runs a group of ordinary dispatched tasks under one versioned strategy, and owns the group-level facts a single task cannot: one pinned base commit, member roles, immutable submitted artifacts, evaluations, a human decision, and a terminal outcome.

founding decision 1

Every member is an ordinary task

No second dispatcher, worktree provisioner, or cancellation path.

founding decision 2

Evaluators recommend, never promote

Nothing destructive happens without a confirmed human decision.

founding decision 3

A run executes its snapshot

The plan is frozen at creation. A run a newer build cannot read loads and reports itself unreadable rather than running differently.

founding decision 4

Members never push

No pushes, no pull requests, no shipping gate. The prompt says so, and the roster is enforced.

The three strategies

StrategyRosterEvaluationOutcome
Best of N2-5 candidates, same task, same commit, aloneOne tool-less anonymous comparison ranks the submissionsA recommended winner you confirm. The default.
Consensus3-5 attemptsOne anonymous pass compares what the submissions decided - shared decisions become agreements, each divergence an open question with one option per position actually taken. It may not rank, score, or recommend.Nothing promoted, nothing reaped; the run terminates retained.
Panel vote2-5 candidates2-5 independent single-lens judges - a rubric (Correctness, Maintainability, Risk, Evidence, Scope) or a catalog Persona, snapshotted at creation. Two judges may not share a rubric. All asked in parallel against one shared anonymous packet.Borda ranking over ranks, at a quorum of two usable ballots.

Hard ceilings no strategy can exceed: 16 members, 8 concurrent, 8 waves, 5 stage attempts. Review launch posts a side-effect-free preview - member count, concurrency, waves, evaluation calls, whether the chosen workflow mode is executable - and any later edit invalidates the green Reviewed chip, so Launch N agents confirms exactly what was reviewed.

Running and submitting

The runtime pins one full base commit and launches bounded waves of ordinary member tasks - creating every task in a wave before dispatching the first, never exceeding the authorized concurrency. Titles start with Candidate N - so siblings stay identifiable.

submit_ensemble_result is a launch precondition: a member launch is refused before the agent spawns unless the MCP bundle both registers and actually publishes the tool, verified by a real handshake - because a member that finishes and cannot signal it stalls the whole run.

The submission tool carries only bounded claims - summary (required), checks[] ("do not claim a check you did not run"), testEvidence - and no ids at all: the daemon attributes calling session → task → active member, so a guessed id reaches nothing. Submission captures the working tree through a temporary git index, never the member's real one, leaving its staged/unstaged split, HEAD, branch and tree byte-identical, and writes an immutable commit under a private refs/mission-control/ensembles/<id>/<artifact> ref. Diffs are re-derived on demand in three sizes (whole patch, one file, file list), with statistics complete in every answer. Barriers advance off ready artifacts, not off a task going idle.

Judging blind

Best of N and Panel vote evaluate when every live member has submitted or terminated and at least two produced a snapshot; Consensus needs at least three. The packet carries the task, bounded base-to-snapshot diffs, per-file statistics and each member's own claims (labelled as claims) - with every agent name, model, ordinal, ref name, snapshot commit id and worktree path stripped and each submission relabelled anonymously. Candidate-authored sections are fenced as untrusted; truncated diff evidence is disclosed.

Replies are validated strictly: exactly the eligible submissions once each, integer scores, contiguous ranks, a recommendation holding rank 1. Anything malformed, incomplete, or injected is a failed attempt - never a low score and never a fallback winner. In Panel vote each judge that reaches a provider call gets its own evaluation row, and a malformed reply fails that row only. The stage succeeds at a quorum of two usable ballots; below quorum it retries whole against the same submissions up to the attempt cap, and a panel that never reaches quorum fails the run - one surviving ballot is never the answer, because its disagreement measure is vacuously zero. Ranking is Borda points over each judge's ranks, never over the 0-100 scores, computed by one shared function the daemon and the dashboard both call. A submission missing from a readable ballot contributes nothing rather than a worst-place score. Ties are declared, not resolved.

Decision and finalization

States run planning → running → waiting → evaluating → awaiting_decision → finalizing → completed, plus cancelling, cancelled, failed. A confirmed decision carries a stable request id, the expected run state, and an explicit destructive confirmation. Only then does anything destructive run, restart-safe and in order:

  1. Re-verify the winner's private ref resolves. A missing ref blocks all cleanup.
  2. Make one exact winner available - either Restored (the member's own session reset to its snapshot) or Replacement (one new task <run title> - selected result provisioned at the snapshot, with the original settled done and its worktree deliberately kept until a confirmed Clean up).
  3. Reap every loser through normal task cancellation.
  4. Then either hand the winner to a pinned published workflow version or type it one continuation - never both.

Every loser's private snapshot survives, and there is no time-based pruning - only an explicit Delete ensemble, irreversible, with the id echoed in the body.

Where they show up

Every candidate wears an E mark (distinct from a workflow's W) reading e.g. E 3/5 · working, or attention-toned needs an answer. Siblings are ordered adjacent in Cards and grouped under a cluster header in Board and the Console rail, with one progress square per roster lane - amber waiting-on-you, green submitted, blue working, red lost, outlined unopened - as counts, not positions, plus an N needs you / outlined N elsewhere rollup. A cluster never crosses a Board tone column. Stage vocabulary is one set of words everywhere: launching, working, reviewing, waiting on you, promoting, done/cancelled/failed, unreadable.

#/ensembles lists every run attention-first from one event stream; #/ensembles/:id is the full dossier - the Launch → Work → Review → Decide → Promote pipeline with its barrier stated in words, live member lanes (tone, activity, goal, elapsed, honest last-event age, live cost, Withdraw / Retry / Submit / Open session / Open task, and in-place answering of blocking asks), the immutable artifacts with on-demand diffs, the timeline, the strategy's own result view (candidate columns / agreement and divergence cards / rank matrix and ballots), Compare (a churn-sorted file-touch matrix plus synchronized side-by-side panes for two or three candidates), and the one-shot decision form beneath the evidence.

09How it fits together

Read the features separately and they look like six products. They are not: they are one pipeline with one human at the decision points. This is the shape of it.

The properties that recur

Read enough of this codebase and the same handful of decisions keep reappearing. They are worth naming, because they are what the product actually is:

01

Never claim what you cannot prove

A dispatch that cannot prove it started fails. A PR action completes on an observed pull request at the exact commit, never because the session said so. A Command that did not run says "Skipped" and why. An uncertain terminal delivery says delivery uncertain and offers Retry.

02

Infrastructure failure is not a verdict

A timeout, a malformed reply, a provider outage - these block or retry. They never become "the reviewer said no", and they never become a low score or a fallback winner.

03

Consent is separate from capability

Foreman invites, the Trust allowlist, Inspector adoption, the workflow-Commands double gate, the plan skills check. Being able to act is never permission to act.

04

Repository content is untrusted input

Evidence is fenced in every prompt. Prior reviewer feedback is labelled non-human. A memory index symlinked out of the tree is ignored. Secrets are scrubbed from every outbound string.

05

One writer, one source of truth

The daemon is the only database writer - Foreman goes over loopback HTTP. One function prices every automation run. One predicate decides whether a retro is offered. One function computes Borda points for both the daemon and the dashboard.

06

State is a word, not a colour

Complete / Partial / Unreadable. Off - nothing is being reviewed. Enabled, but no worker is running. Autopilot off - nothing starts unless you start it. Empty states say which kind of empty they are.

Getting there from here

npm install
npm run build
npm run dev          # daemon + dashboard on 127.0.0.1:7317
npm run foreman      # optional: the autonomous operator, separate process
npm run demo -- --fresh   # a fully isolated fleet where every agent binary is
                          # a scripted scenario player - spends no tokens

Everything is local: SQLite at ~/.mission-control/harness.db, archives beside it, the whole state root relocatable with MISSION_HOME. Nothing about a session, an archive, or a memory leaves the machine except the two things you explicitly point outward - the GitHub Inspector's comments, and a task pushed to GitHub as an issue.

10What this guide does not establish

Stated plainly, because a guide that only claims is not evidence.

  • This is a code-and-docs reading, not a field test. Behaviour is drawn from the repository's own documentation and source at commit 4438b563, cross-checked against the running dashboard. It is not a report on how the product behaves under a week of real load, and it measures nothing.
  • The screenshots are of a deliberately token-free demo fleet. Every agent binary is replaced by a scripted scenario player, so the conversations, diffs and workflow verdicts are real Mission Control surfaces driven by fake agents. Consequences visible in the frames: the workflow's Command gates read Skipped because no command is configured on that machine, the Foreman worker is not running, no task sources are configured, and the Runs / Ensembles / Scouts pages start empty. The Scouts figure is the committed documentation capture, which has archives seeded; the rest are fresh.
  • Foreman's live behaviour is not shown. Its posture and controls are; a real escalation brief, a real cheap-tier divergence row, and a real queue drain are not - those need a running worker spending real tokens against a real fleet.
  • No ensemble run is shown end to end. The launch surface and its plan are; the member lanes, the anonymized ballots, the rank matrix, and the Compare view are described from the code and the docs/ensembles.md contract rather than photographed.
  • Pipelines (external SDLC engines) are out of scope here beyond the pipeline task kind. That subsystem has its own reference and its own failure modes.
  • Nothing here is a security review. Several boundaries are quoted - the untrusted-input fencing, the Inspector's path deny rules, the Jira host restriction, the archive parser's refusals - but they are quoted, not tested.
  • Version drift is real. The built-in workflow is on version 10 with nine preserved predecessors, and the Library, the Line and the settings taxonomy have all been reorganized more than once. Exact ids and route spellings are stable contracts; screen arrangements are not.
